description: We're building Moto View, a Tanzania burning-activity calendar for the MODIS & VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. We harmonize two satellite fire records so over a decade of burning can be explored on one consistent calendar. We have the data and coding side covered and want a third teammate for stats/remote sensing, UI design, or pitch storytelling. Beginners welcome. Come ship a working demo with us. We are in Kenya. We chose Tanzania because it is close by and has higher fire rates than Kenya.
summary: FireWatch is a harmonized burning-activity calendar for Tanzania that combines NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into one consistent record from 2000 to 2026(June). Because the sensors differ in pixel size, sensitivity, and start dates, raw hotspot counts create a false jump when VIIRS begins in 2012. We place both sensors on a 0.25° grid, using fire-days as a bridge, and calibrate VIIRS counts to MODIS-equivalent hotspot counts during the overlapping years. Held-out validation reports correlation, bias, error, and uncertainty rather than hiding it. A static web app allows users draw an area or enter coordinates, choose a date range, and explore a year-by-month calendar, raw and harmonized comparisons, seasonal anomalies, and have downloadable CSV/PNG outputs. By turning two incompatible satellite records into one defensible time series, FireWatch would give fire managers, researchers, and responders a reliable way to see when and where burning has occurred and how current activity compares with the historical baseline. The same pipeline can scale to other regions or global coverage.
details:
FireWatch is a harmonized burning-activity calendar for Tanzania that makes MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records directly comparable from 2000 through mid-2026.

Since the sensors differ in pixel size, sensitivity, overpass times, and start dates, simply joining them creates a false jump when VIIRS begins in 2012. Our pipeline filters and deduplicates NASA FIRMS detections, places both sensors on a common 0.25° grid, counts hotspots and fire-days, and calibrates VIIRS fire-days to MODIS-equivalent hotspot counts using the overlapping years.

We fit the calibration on 2012–2018 and test on 2019–2025, reporting correlation, bias, mean absolute error, annual-total error, and scatter rather than hiding uncertainty.

Benefits and impact

The result is one defensible time series that reflects real changes in burning rather than changes in instrumentation.

A static web app lets users draw an area or enter coordinates and a date range, then explore a year-by-month calendar, compare raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and harmonized views, see seasonal anomalies and headline figures, and download aggregate or capped raw CSV files and a calendar PNG.

This supports:

  • early-warning teams,
  • land managers,
  • firefighters,
  • scientists,
  • the public

In understanding when and where burning has occurred and how current activity compares with the historical baseline. The same workflow can scale to other regions or global coverage.

Tools and technology

We used Python with

  1. Polars
  2. NumPy
  3. SciPy
  4. Matplotlib
  5. React
  6. Leaflet and Leaflet.draw for the map
  7. ECharts for the calendar and charts
  8. gzipped JSON
  9. GitHub
